title: Federal disaster spending can change which firms survive and expand after floods
source_unit: Census CES Working Paper 26-52 using confidential plant-level Census microdata and federally declared flood event studies
geography: United States; plants affected by large federally declared floods, surviving and entering firms, machinery, employment, and federal disaster spending

observations.period: Large federally declared floods and post-disaster recovery; paper published August 2026

denominator.unit: plant-level event-study analysis of flood-affected U.S. firms

exit.value: exits were concentrated among the least productive plants

asset_reallocation.value: used machines from exiting plants were acquired by higher-productivity entrants

survivor_upgrade.value: surviving plants upgraded machinery as they rebuilt and experienced productivity gains

federal_spending.value: federal disaster spending expanded financing access for nimble young and small firms and facilitated productive reallocation

fiscal_result.value: the study reports relative income gains from federal disaster assistance generating tax revenues exceeding upfront policy cost

observations.method: The author uses confidential plant-level Census microdata and an event-study design around large federally declared floods to trace plant exits, machinery transfers, survivor investment, productivity, financing access, and federal disaster spending.
observations.uncertainty: This is a Census CES working paper and not a Census Bureau endorsement. Plant productivity and reallocation do not establish household recovery, worker welfare, local service continuity, or that every closure was socially beneficial; the fiscal conclusion depends on the study's model and measured income effects.
observations.subgroup: Flood-affected plants, less productive exits, higher-productivity entrants, survivors, young and small firms, and places receiving federal disaster spending; effects may differ by industry, local labor market, ownership, household exposure, and disaster severity.
observations.counterinterpretation: Creative destruction can coexist with bankruptcy, lost jobs, debt, displacement, market concentration, delayed rebuilding, or public-service loss. Entrant productivity does not guarantee local hiring or shared gains, and federal financing can select some firms while leaving others behind.

related_sources.claim: The official paper provides the plant-level event-study design, exit and machinery reallocation evidence, survivor productivity, financing mechanism, and fiscal interpretation.

boundary: This record adds a disaster-to-firm-reallocation and public-finance pathway. It does not establish household recovery, worker welfare, equal rebuilding, local service continuity, or that creative destruction is beneficial for every affected community.
